title: Wolverine Wasn't Always a Mutant — Marvel Almost Made Him an Actual Animal
youtube_description:
Wolverine wasn't born the mutant you know. Marvel rewrote him at least three times before he became the guy with bone claws under an adamantium coating.

He first appeared in The Incredible Hulk #180 (October 1974) as a nameless secret agent for the Canadian government — not a mutant, not an X-Man, just a villain with claws built into his gloves. Writer Len Wein and Marvel art director John Romita Sr. designed him with retractable metal blades in his gauntlets, not organic claws.

A year later, Wein and artist Dave Cockrum rewrote him into a mutant and recruited him into a brand-new lineup in Giant-Size X-Men #1 (May 1975) — the same issue that saved the X-Men franchise from cancellation. But that wasn't the final word: after Wein left the ongoing series, Cockrum and incoming writer Chris Claremont floated an idea to make Wolverine an actual mutated wolverine, engineered by the same Marvel scientist behind half of Marvel's animal-human hybrids, the High Evolutionary. Stan Lee reportedly called the concept disgusting and killed it before it reached the page.

It took the Weapon X story (Marvel Comics Presents #72–84, 1991) to explain how his skeleton got bonded with adamantium, and Fatal Attractions (X-Men #25, 1993) — nineteen years after his first appearance — for readers to actually see the bone claws underneath. The “natural mutant” everyone assumes he always was took almost two decades of rewrites to arrive.

This channel digs up the buried production history behind Marvel's biggest characters — subscribe for the retcons even longtime fans never hear about.

Sources: Wikipedia (Wolverine); CBR (“When Wolverine Was Going to Be an Actual Mutated Wolverine,” citing Dave Cockrum's interview with Peter Sanderson in X-Men Companion); Marvel.com (“How 1975's Giant-Size X-Men Saved Marvel's Merry Mutants”).
